Flax.—Irish markets still remain small and all Flax marketed has been bought up. Demand is better, but there is practically no change in value, the tendency being against buyers. On the Continent French Spinners are buying more freely, which has stopped any further fall in value.
Latvian Flax.—There has been no change in quotations during the last fortnight; in fact the exchange has rather stiffened them. Thers are reports of big negotiation pending at present which would steady this market if the business comes off.

label: text
text: Esthonian Flax—Little going prices quietly steady.

label: text
text: Weavers.—There seems to be a rather steadier feeling in the market, but there is not much business being placed. There are a good many small orders being distributed over the various qualities. Damask in the low end shows no sign of improvement, but in the fine end more business has been placed, and there is a much healthier feeling in this section. Manufacturers are busy completing old contracts for Dress. Linen, most of which require to be completed by the end of next month. Merchants.—Housekeeping Goods. In actual business placed there is not much to say since last report Conditions at present need careful attention on the part both of buyers and sellers. In the general line of Housekeeping goods values offered are based on bare manufacturing costs, and do not represent anything in the way of margin to Merchants. These prices can hardly be repeated, if orders come forward in the usual quantity for Spring business. In Cambrics and Sheers there is likely to be a revision which will reduce the low numbers and bring them into line for more attractive selling prices in Domestic Handerchiefs. Medium and better numbers are to-day selling at closest margin possible, and are perfectly safe for forward buying.

label: text
text: Soviet Flax.--The Continent is taking more interest but as these prices have been reduced very little from the height, business is difficult to arrange.

label: text
text: Dress Linens - Important shipments for U.S.A., and other markets have been made during the past fortnight and some moderate sized orders have been arranged. A general improvement in business is expected during March.

label: text
text: The British Tea Shares Trust, which was incorporated as a private company some 12 years ago and converted into a public company recently has applied to the London Stock Exchange for permission for the shares to be dealt in. Not infrequently action of this kind is the forerunner of an invitation to the public to subscribe new capital. The authorized capital of the trust is £50,000 divided into £1 shares, of which half have been issued and are fully paid up. The present directors are R. B. Fidler and Thomas Pickett.

label: text
text: The Assam Co. is paying an interim dividend of 7½%, less tax on a capital of £1,000,000. This is at the rate of 1s. 6d. a share. The interim dividend declared last year was 15%, which was on the old capital, and equals 3% on the present amount.

label: text

label: text
text: The Ceylon & Indian Planters' Association, for the year ending June 30 made a gross profit of £27,664, as against £30,108 in 1922-23. Interest receipts were £800, and £4,489 was brought forward. Debenture interest and fixed charges take £4,132; depreciation and cost of ten extensions amount to £1,096. Preference dividend stands at £1,500, and £1,000 is put to income tax account; £5,000 is placed to the general reserve. The proposed final dividend of 20% on the ordinary shares makes the rate for the year 30%, the same as for the preceding year. The balance carried forward is £5,440. The tea crop of 784,298 pounds shows an increase of 16,984 pounds.

label: text
text: Trading in the cotton markets has been more active and American values have advanced steadily. A sound undertone has been in general evidence owing to the fact that there has been no decrease in the larger absorption of cotton by the world's consumers. American advices report a continued strong demand for spot; Liverpool sales have been fairly good; and steadily advancing premiums have been paid for deliveries before the end of the season. New crop months have also been well supported owing to the lateness of preparations for want of rain. There is still time to retrieve this loss of time but reports have been much more insistent and serious in tone, and a certain amount of nervousness has been created as to the possibility of another inadequate crop. Mainly in consequence of this heavy buying has taken place and in all the advance has totalled ½d per lb. The Egyptian section has been quiet and prices are practically unchanged. In the Manchester market hopes have not been fulfilled. There has been a fair volume of enquiry but although the smaller outlets have again made a moderate showing they have not made up for the lack of business from the large Far Eastern markets which is now unusually late. The low selling prices ruling in these markets and the unsatisfactory, offtake is still apparently absorbing more attention than new business. There are purchasers who appear to be looking ahead more but they are few. It is very likely, however, that these few will prove to have bought well. American yarns have been in active demand but spinners have been barely able to obtain the full advance in the raw material. Medium Egyptians have been in better request but super grades are practically neglected and prices are unaltered. India has been quiet beyond a fair enquiry for dhootics, light whites, prints and fancies. China has enquired for fancies and dyed goods with poor results. Singapore and Java have been fairly prominent for miscellaneous styles. The Continent, Africa and South America have also done a small trade.

label: text
text: While the cotton spinners are considering the question of working shorter hours, the news comes of big Russian orders for Lancashire which are being placed by the Soviet Government representatives with authority, it is stated, to place orders running into many millions of pounds weight for delivery between now and next September.

label: text
text: One substantial order for 400,000 pounds' weight of yarn and waste has already been booked by the Astley Mills Company, Manchester which will keep three large mills at Dukinfield running until the end of March.

label: text
text: Germany is going into the soap business in Holland. It has acquired the plant of the former Zwarte Rutter brewery at Manairicht as well as the plant of a soap factory there. The two are to be combined into a larger chemical plant which is to manufacture soap, soda and castor oil.

label: text
text: German hotel and restaurant proprietors are considering the possibilities of moving pictures on the premises as producers of trade. They argue that as there are no free passes to the movies, a condition that prevails largely among the theatres, the man who goes to the movies probably has money to spend for refreshments. Hence, if they could once get him on the lot, they would stand a fair chance of selling him something more than his movie ticket.
